newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania pushes to resolve pyramid loss before vote.
newsitem.headline: Albania pushes to resolve pyramid loss before vote.

text.p: Representatives of Albania and international financial institutions will meet in Rome next week to assess losses from shady pyramid investment schemes which collapsed and sparked riots that devastated the Balkan country, Finance Minister Arben Malaj said on Thursday.
But he held out little hope of people ever again seeing much of the estimated $1.2 billion that had been invested in the schemes, saying "Albania is too poor and the amounts of losses are too big".

He told Reuters in an interview that the purpose of the meeting was to assess the loss, try to get a recovery programme under way and to defuse tensions in advance of early elections to replace an interim government installed after President Sali Berisha was forced to dissolve his Democratic Party cabinet.

"What we are concerned about is the disillusion of the people who have put money into the schemes and for this we need cooperation at the highest level of all the international institutions to find possible ways to soften that disillusion," said Malaj, a member of the Socialist Party which is the main opposition to Berisha's Democrats.

The collapse of five pyramid investments schemes earlier this year touched off rioting and looting in March which wrecked many businesses. Malaj said that as a result gross domestic product should decline by three to seven percent this year, from an IMF estimate of $2.8 billion in 1996.

He said the meeting in Rome from Monday to Wednesday would include legal representatives of the interim government of national reconciliation, the presidency and international financial institutions, including the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

"What we want is before the elections to give some basic indications about all these companies, first of all to take steps to prevent any misleading (of the public) by those few funds that still exist, to find out what assets they still have and to make a kind of inventory which will be handed onto the new government," he said.
"We want the people before the elections to know what the prospects are for getting back their money," he added.

He said that at the same time the government, beset by sharp declines in customs duties that usually provide half of government revenues, plus other losses from the riots, hopes to get a recovery plan in place.
He said the main elements of the plan were providing unemployment assistance, aid for shelter, credits for private businesses and opening investment credit lines.

He said the international community had been providing Albania, Europe's poorest country, with roughly $260 million a year in assistance before the riots disrupted many programmes and that the country's needs now were "much, much more".
He said customs and value added tax collections were running at 35 to 40 percent of normal, because of widespread destruction of customs offices.
